item.title: Image Text Extraction Pipeline: VLMs, KV Soft-Reset, and Legal Evidence from Phone Screenshots
item.description:
Phone screenshots are not evidence in a useful form. They are unreadable at scale, unsearchable, easy to lose, and impossible to cross-reference precisely. This project builds a four-stage pipeline that turns hundreds of raw screenshots — HEIC photos of Teams chats, Outlook emails, Copilot sessions — into clean, structured, court-ready PDF documents.

The engineering challenges are interesting: the images are tall and narrow; the content scrolls, producing overlapping captures; the model must never invent; and the entire pipeline runs on a consumer GPU with 6 GB of true VRAM and a CPU with 32 GB of DDR4.

item.title: Image Text Extraction v2: Event-Driven Pipeline Architecture
item.description:
The v1 pipeline solved the problem. v2 redesigns the solution as a proper software system — one that is testable, composable, and maintainable. The core algorithms are unchanged; the architecture around them is rebuilt from scratch using dependency injection, an event-driven stage model, and a standalone toolkit library that carries no mandatory runtime dependencies.

item.title: Cooper's Way
item.description:
Architectural Principles & Engineering Directives Link to heading

Complex distributed systems, whether pricing equity derivatives or orchestrating asynchronous browser workers, tend to degrade when incidental complexity is introduced under the guise of cleverness. Over decades of designing and delivering platforms for global financial institutions, I have refined Cooper’s Way—a unified set of architectural directives, concurrency invariants, and coding standards designed to keep software deterministic, observable, and easy to maintain.

item.title: Murex Capital Markets AI Agent & LLM Proxy
item.description:
Domain-Calibrated Enterprise AI for Capital Markets Link to heading

Trading platforms such as Murex MX.3 form the core computational backbone of tier-one investment banks, governing trade booking, market risk, and post-trade lifecycle workflows. However, configuring, troubleshooting, and operating these platforms requires specialized institutional knowledge spanning financial mathematics, proprietary scripting syntaxes, and complex database schemas.

In institutional banking environments, operational workflows must comply with stringent communication and compliance policies. Commercial messaging tools are strictly prohibited for trade-related discussions; all communication must flow through monitored, bank-approved collaboration infrastructure.

item.title: High-Performance Go Systems & Data Pipelines
item.description:
Zero-Allocation Stream Processing and Data Ingestion Link to heading

Processing multi-gigabyte personal data archives and high-volume email mailboxes presents significant memory management and resilience challenges. In-memory object deserialization quickly leads to GC pauses, memory exhaustion, and unrecoverable failures when batch jobs crash midway through execution. This project encompasses a suite of high-throughput CLI utilities, concurrent stream parsers, and data ingestion microservices engineered in Go to achieve deterministic memory bounds, sub-millisecond inter-process communication, and resume-safe state execution.

item.title: Enterprise Chromium Extension Ecosystem
item.description:
High-Throughput Concurrency in Manifest V3 Link to heading

Modern browser extensions operating under the Chromium Manifest V3 specification face strict architectural constraints: ephemeral service worker lifecycles, background execution quotas, and the constant risk of saturating the browser main thread during heavy data processing. This project is a monorepo ecosystem of five standalone Chromium extensions powered by a shared core kernel that provides deterministic task scheduling, dynamic worker pool auto-scaling, and persistent state recovery.

item.title: Production Equity Swap Pricing Engine
item.description:
High-Performance Equity Derivative Valuation in C# Link to heading

Valuing complex financial derivatives requires bridging two conflicting engineering paradigms: low-level, high-throughput quantitative calculation libraries and high-level, maintainable enterprise domain architectures. Many quantitative engines expose unmanaged, handle-based APIs that rely on manual memory marshaling, implicit ordering conventions, and untyped pointer structures. When exposed directly to application developers, these interfaces lead to memory leaks, invalid state combinations, and unrepeatable calculation runs.

item.title: Reconciliation Engine
item.description:

Reconciliation Framework Link to heading

The Reconciliation Engine is a modular batch-processing framework designed to execute named reconciliation routines with precision and operational clarity. Built in Java and powered by Spring’s XML-based context configuration, the engine allows for dynamic resolution of reconciliation logic at runtime using a provider pattern. This design enables flexible orchestration of reconciliation workflows without requiring changes to the core application.

item.title: Service Framework
item.description:
browse this repository

Service Framework Link to heading

The Service Framework enables the development of event-based services to orchestrate BAU workflows. It provides a declarative, annotation-driven model for defining service behavior, routing logic, and execution conditions—all within a Spring Boot environment. By abstracting the complexities of event handling and service discovery, it allows developers to focus on core business logic while maintaining a highly decoupled architecture.

item.title: Identity‑Anchored Encryption
item.description:
Identity-Centric Security Model Link to heading

This project demonstrates how encryption can be made identity‑centric — shifting control from purely key‑based systems to ones anchored in user identity and consent. Each record is encrypted with its own random key, which is then wrapped with the user’s public key. Even if one key is compromised, only that single record is exposed.

Decryption is never an automatic process. Instead, it is governed by a multi‑step verification sequence that begins with a valid identity token (JWT) issued by Okta. If the actor requesting access is not the original data owner, the system triggers an explicit user approval workflow. Only after identity is verified and consent is granted does the Key Management Service attempt to unwrap the record’s unique encryption key.

item.title: Permissions Application Suite
item.description:
The Permissions Application Suite is a cutting-edge solution that enables efficient and scalable permission, directory group, and management group handling in modern enterprise systems. It consists of two complementary components, the Permissions Admin and the Permissions Service, combined with a focus on leveraging Angular, React design principles, and TypeScript. This suite provides an advanced framework for handling complex workflows, ensuring precise access control and improving developer efficiency.

Overview of Permissions Application Suite Link to heading

The Permissions Admin serves as the modular, responsive frontend interface, enabling administrators to manage permissions dynamically through an interactive and user-friendly Angular-based interface. It empowers enterprise teams to configure roles and groups intuitively.

item.title: Cloud Cost Optimisation & Platform Engineering
item.description:
Cloud cost is rarely a billing problem — it is an architecture and operational discipline problem. The savings delivered here came from eliminating waste built into the platform’s foundations: over-provisioned compute, manual deployment processes that required bespoke configuration per environment, and a lack of shared tooling that caused every team to solve the same infrastructure problems independently.

The work spanned three interconnected areas: right-sizing and tuning the Kubernetes workloads running on AWS EKS, designing and delivering a versioned CI/CD framework that was subsequently adopted across multiple teams, and architecting the broader AWS environment — an architecture reviewed by AWS and assessed as highly scalable and well-designed.

item.title: Reinforcement Learning & Autonomous Agents
item.description:
Reinforcement Learning (RL) represents a fundamental shift in how machines learn. Unlike supervised learning, where a model is provided with a “ground truth” label for every input, an RL agent must discover which actions yield the highest reward by interacting with a dynamic environment.

I developed a set of autonomous agents capable of navigating complex, stochastic environments. This project explores the transition from traditional Q-learning to Deep Q-Networks (DQN) and the integration of physical laws into the learning process through Physics-Informed Reinforcement Learning (PIRL).

item.title: Distributed Training Infrastructure: Scaling to GPT-2
item.description:
Scaling from toy-sized Transformers to Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-2 is a fundamental engineering challenge. At this scale, the primary bottleneck is no longer just mathematical correctness—it is hardware memory bandwidth, interconnect latency, and computational throughput.

I designed and implemented a professional-grade training infrastructure capable of training a 124M parameter GPT-2 model. This project involved orchestrating multi-GPU clusters, maximizing FLOPS through mixed-precision arithmetic, and managing massive data streams for billions of tokens.

item.title: Transformer Architecture: Building GPT-2 from Scratch
item.description:
The Transformer architecture is the engine behind modern generative AI. Unlike previous sequential models (RNNs) or hierarchical models (WaveNets) that rely on fixed patterns, the Transformer uses Self-Attention to dynamically weight the importance of every token in a sequence relative to every other token.

I built a complete Transformer decoder—the same architecture used in the GPT family—from the ground up. This project involved implementing the core attention mechanism, modular multi-head blocks, and the engineering required to stabilize deep residual networks.

item.title: Professional PyTorch Workflow: Engineering Patterns
item.description:
In the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence, there is a fundamental distinction between merely writing a script and architecting a solution. A professional AI workflow requires more than just calling .train(); it demands a rigorous, reproducible framework that covers the entire lifecycle of a model—from hardware-agnostic data orchestration to deterministic performance monitoring.

I developed a robust PyTorch engineering workflow designed for discovery and reliability. This project outlines the core pillars of my approach to building high-performance AI systems.

item.title: Language Modelling
item.description:
To predict the next character or word in a sequence, a model must “remember” what came before. I explored this progression from first principles, starting with basic statistical counting and evolving into deep, hierarchical neural architectures that capture complex linguistic structures.

This project covers the transition from frequentist models to neural-based optimization, the introduction of continuous embeddings, and the engineering required to stabilize deep networks.

The Problem: The Curse of Dimensionality Link to heading

In a simple Bigram Model, we predict the next character based solely on the current one. If we have 27 possible characters (a-z plus space), we can store all possible transitions in a $27 \times 27$ lookup table.

item.title: Building a Scalar-Valued Autograd Engine from First Principles
item.description:
Modern deep learning frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow abstract away the complex calculus involved in model training. While efficient, this abstraction can lead to a “black box” understanding of how models actually learn. To bridge this gap, I built a fully functional, scalar-valued automatic differentiation engine from scratch.

This engine, which I’ve termed my “Value Engine,” implements backpropagation over a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) and supports the training of multi-layer perceptrons (MLP) using only basic Python and scalar math.

item.title: AI / ML Systems
item.description:
This section explores my work in AI architecture, deep learning, and reinforcement learning – with a focus on first-principles engineering, behavioral signal extraction, and agentic orchestration. My approach treats AI as a composable extension of core infrastructure, engineered for reproducibility, clarity, and strategic reuse.

Neural Engineering & First Principles Link to heading

I develop foundational models from scratch using PyTorch, moving beyond black-box implementations to master the mechanics of backpropagation, custom layer normalization, and hierarchical embedding pipelines. This includes building context-based token predictors using MLPs, implementing stable training loops with manual gradient updates, and visualizing latent spaces to track how models represent information. These projects are designed for architectural transparency, allowing for full introspection into data flow and gradient propagation.

item.title: AI Engineering: Core Concepts & Technical Deep Dive
item.description:
This page provides a technical consolidation of the core principles encountered across the AI engineering landscape. Rather than a simple collection of definitions, this guide serves as a narrative reference for the essential components of modern deep learning, tracing the path from fundamental calculus and statistical bigrams to the distributed orchestration of large-scale transformer models.

The driving insight is that sophisticated AI behaviour is built on a foundation of “first principles” engineering. By understanding the local derivative, we unlock the global gradient; by mastering initialisation and normalisation, we stabilise the signal; and by engineering for hardware efficiency, we scale these principles to the level of human language.

item.title: Best Practice
item.description:
General Engineering Principles Link to heading

The Foundation: Four Principles Every Codebase Needs Link to heading

Good software starts with four principles that work together. The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) says that every module, class, and function should have exactly one reason to change. When a unit handles multiple concerns, a change in one area risks breaking another, and tests become difficult to reason about because behaviour spans unrelated paths. Keeping things focused makes refactoring safe and failures easy to isolate.

item.title: Cloud Technology
item.description:
Cloud Technology Link to heading

This section documents my work in cloud-native architecture, infrastructure-as-code, and serverless orchestration — with a focus on reproducibility, runtime clarity, and strategic reuse across AWS and Azure.

I build systems that treat cloud infrastructure as programmable, observable, and modular — engineered for fault tolerance, secure delivery, and operational transparency.

AWS & Azure Architecture Link to heading

I’ve designed and delivered robust, cloud‑native platforms across both AWS and Azure, supporting everything from high‑frequency trading systems and reconciliation engines to AI‑enabled orchestration layers. My AWS expertise spans a wide range of services, including compute with EC2 and Lambda, storage and databases via S3 and RDS, and advanced orchestration using Step Functions, API Gateway, and EKS. On the Azure side, I’ve implemented solutions using AKS, Azure Functions, and Key Vault, ensuring that all platforms are built for runtime introspection, secure delivery, and multi‑region resilience.

item.title: Coder Instructions
item.description:
Role and Scope Link to heading

  • Act strictly as the Professional Software Engineer executing Planner specs; do not assume other roles.
  • Implement interfaces-first, follow SOLID, and produce clean, testable code.
  • Do not re-plan, reinterpret, or modify planning files.
  • Read-only planning input: reference/documentation/planning/plan.md.
  • Maintain internal notes only in out/coder.notes (never used as documentation).

Execution Rules Link to heading

  • Execute exactly what each subtask specifies; do not add features or refactor unrelated code.
  • Implement only the scope defined in the current subtask.
  • Assume interfaces are correct; treat them as the source of truth over implementations.
  • Always define interfaces/protocols before implementations and use dependency injection.
  • Keep imports at the top of files; use absolute imports; no dynamic or in-function imports.
  • Never use placeholder comments like # ...existing code...; integrate changes inline.
  • Prefer pure functions for transformations; isolate side effects at infrastructure boundaries.
  • Use OOP with interfaces for stateful or polymorphic behaviour; use pure functions for deterministic transforms.
  • Apply well-known patterns (Factory, Strategy, Adapter, Facade, Builder, Composite, Visitor) only when justified.
  • Use language-native async/streaming APIs (generators, async iterators, streams) for concurrency; avoid manual subscription management.

Size, Complexity, and Organisation Link to heading

  • Classes: preferably fewer than 10 methods.
  • Functions: preferably fewer than 20 lines.
  • Files: preferably fewer than 500 lines (aim around 250).
  • Keep modules cohesive and focused; avoid god-objects and god-modules.
  • Structure code by functionality and domain; expose only what is required externally.
  • Reuse shared utilities; check for existing implementations before adding new code.
  • Update dependency files when adding dependencies.

Logging, Errors, and Exceptions Link to heading

  • Use structured logging when logging is required; do not use print for debugging unless explicitly specified.
  • Do not swallow exceptions; handle, log, or propagate with specific exception types.
  • Use specific exception classes; never use bare except:.
  • Fail fast on invalid input and provide contextual error messages.

Tests and Quality Link to heading

  • Follow AAA (Arrange, Act, Assert) with explicit # Arrange, # Act, # Assert comments.
  • One test class per source class; one test method per use case.
  • Tests must be isolated with mocks and fail fast.
  • Include explicit assertions for happy, empty, invalid, and boundary cases.
  • Test classes must extend unittest.TestCase and use its lifecycle and assertion methods.
  • Apply marble testing for reactive logic where relevant.
  • Keep tests fast and focused; place tests alongside source code and mirror the package structure.

Documentation and Temp Files Link to heading

  • Add docstrings only for public APIs when required by the plan.
  • When documentation is requested, write human-readable paragraphs describing what was done, not future plans.
  • Temporary output must go to out/**/* and be cleaned up when no longer needed.
  • Create scripts only with explicit permission and place them in reference/scripts/**/*.

Change-log Rules Link to heading

  • After each subtask, append a single-line entry to reference/documentation/change-log.md.
  • Newest entries must be at the top of the file.
  • Format: - YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ - [Subtask ID] - [File(s) Modified] - [Action] - [Summary of what was done] - [Lines Added/Modified/Deleted]
  • Example: - 2026-03-02T14:30:00Z - Task 3.2 Subtask 1 - file_tree.py, test_file_tree.py - Implemented FileTree capability and tests - +150 lines

Verification Checklist Link to heading

Before marking a subtask complete, verify:

item.title: Copilot Instructions
item.description:
General Behaviour Link to heading

  • Responses must be short, precise, actionable, and non-verbose.
  • Prefer single-line, machine-parsable bullets for actionable items.
  • Provide concrete examples and explicit expected outputs when needed for clarity.
  • Select the single best option; research externally when correctness requires it.
  • Never run scripts or commands without explicit permission; provide PowerShell commands only when allowed.
  • Never create unnecessary files; only modify or create files explicitly required by the task.
  • Never replace code with placeholder comments (e.g., # ...existing code...).
  • Never expose internal tool names, rate limits, or runtime details.
  • No emojis or images in any files or documentation.

File Structure, Imports, and Code Organisation Link to heading

  • Keep imports at the top of files; do not use dynamic or in-function imports.
  • Follow SOLID, DRY, KISS, and YAGNI.
  • Use interfaces for all classes and services; call implementations only through interfaces.
  • Use dependency injection for service interfaces; avoid unnecessary indirection layers.
  • Prefer immutable parameters, fields, and variables where practical.
  • Keep modules cohesive and loosely coupled with minimal public surface area.
  • Structure code by domain and functionality; do not encode package names into file names.
  • Update dependency files when adding dependencies.
  • Do not add documentation inside code.

Logging, Debugging, and Error Handling Link to heading

  • Use structured logging instead of print.
  • Never hide exceptions; handle, log, or propagate them.
  • Use events and well-defined models to decouple packages and pass data across boundaries.

Tests and Quality Link to heading

  • Tests must follow AAA (Arrange, Act, Assert) with explicit # Arrange, # Act, # Assert comments.
  • Tests must live alongside source code and mirror the package structure.
  • Use one test class per source class and one test method per use case.
  • Use mocks to isolate dependencies and fail fast.
  • Test classes must extend unittest.TestCase and use its lifecycle and assertion methods.
  • Aim for 70-90% coverage; test critical paths and edge cases, not trivial getters/setters.
  • Apply marble testing for reactive logic where relevant.

Documentation, Notes, and Logs Link to heading

  • Notes, logs, and documentation must place newest information at the top.
  • Documentation must be human-readable paragraphs describing what was done (not future plans).
  • Documentation for AI models must use single continuous paragraphs per list item with minimal formatting.
  • Permanent documentation must live under reference/documentation/**/*.
  • Resources must live under reference/resources/**/*.
  • Temporary files must live under out/**/* and must not be committed.
  • PowerShell scripts must live under reference/scripts/**/*.

Issue Handling and Planning Link to heading

  • Do not bypass issues; fix them.
  • Do not ignore failing tests; fix the code or request plan updates.
  • If a file must be deleted, ask the user and provide the exact command.
  • Never bypass the plan; request updates if the plan is incorrect.

AI, RAG, and Model Usage Link to heading

  • Follow .github/best-practice/AI.md for all AI, RAG, and model-related behaviour.
  • Assume interfaces are correct; treat them as the source of truth over implementations.
  • Use lazy loading, batching, and device-aware execution.
  • Use quantisation, mixed precision, and compilation when appropriate.
  • Follow token optimisation and context budgeting rules.
  • Use ONNX, TensorRT, or Torch Compile when beneficial.
  • Never load a model per request; batch by model and process all items before unloading.
  • Always respect machine capabilities defined in machine-capabilities.md.

Documentation for Other AIs Link to heading

  • When generating documentation intended for other AI systems:
    • Use single continuous paragraphs per list item.
    • Avoid heavy Markdown formatting (tables, code blocks, nested bullets).
    • Keep headings minimal.
    • Ensure maximum embedding consistency and retrieval quality.

Restricted Tools Link to heading

  • Do not attempt to use restricted tools: run_in_terminal.

Final Rule Link to heading

  • These instructions apply to the AI only. They do not apply to the human operator.

item.title: Image Classification & Face Recognition System
item.description:
This project was built to bring order to large, mixed‑quality media collections — the kind that blend treasured photos with everyday clutter. It takes a simple list of files and transforms it into a rich, structured dataset that’s easy to search, filter, and work with through an interactive 3D visualisation interface.

The process starts by checking what’s already known about each file and filling in any missing details. It then creates lightweight, high‑quality thumbnails to speed up processing and reduce strain on storage and networks. These thumbnails are cached so they can be reused without repeatedly loading the original files.

item.title: MPC Project Analyser
item.description:
MPC Project Analyser Link to heading

The MPC Project Analyser is a deterministic, batch-based analysis engine written in Python. It bridges the gap between expensive, high-reasoning AI models and cost-effective execution models. Rather than feeding raw source code to every AI agent, the analyser generates compact structural metadata — AST signatures, file trees, documentation maps — that enables agents to plan software changes safely and efficiently without consuming unnecessary context.

item.title: Real‑Time Orchestration Platform
item.description:
This platform is an end-to-end orchestration system for equity derivatives calculation at institutional scale. It coordinates data collection, instrument conversion, pricing calculation, and results publication across multiple AWS services — running continuously against live market positions and publishing structured output downstream for risk management and regulatory reporting.

The platform was architected, built, and delivered from the ground up. All core services, calculations, and infrastructure were designed and implemented as a cohesive, extensible platform — reviewed by AWS and assessed as highly scalable and well-designed.

item.title: Swaps Pricing Engine (MVP)
item.description: The Swaps Pricing Engine is a production-ready C# library that prices total return equity swaps against a proprietary COM-based pricing engine. Rather than exposing the engine’s unmanaged handle-based interfaces directly, the library introduces a thin but complete domain model that maps naturally onto how traders and risk managers think about equity swap contracts and positions. The result is a system that is easy to use correctly and difficult to use incorrectly — enforcing market conventions through the type system, guiding consumers through a fluent API, and validating inputs through a layered rule framework before anything reaches the pricing engine.

item.title: Synthetic Platform Versioning
item.description: A distributed platform is made up of independently deployed components — a Python utility package, an Airflow DAG bundle, a Kubernetes Helm chart, an EC2 application wrapper, API contracts, and supporting scripts. Each component has its own build pipeline and its own version number. The challenge is that when you ask “what is running in production right now?”, you should be able to answer precisely — not just for one service, but for every component simultaneously.
